newsitem.title: ITALY: OLYMPICS-IOC MEDICAL HEAD WANTS SHORTER DOPE BANS.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-IOC MEDICAL HEAD WANTS SHORTER DOPE BANS.

text.p: Current fixed-term sanctions against athletes who fail dope tests should be scrapped in favour of shorter bans, International Olympic Commission (IOC) medical chief Prince Alexandre de Merode said on Wednesday.
"I think the time for fixed suspensions is over. They will always be questioned by the law courts," De Merode told a news conference after a meeting of anti-doping experts.
"What is the point of an inapplicable sanction? Personally, I think we should have shorter suspensions," he said.
"We have also had to adapt to the social evolution in sports. As a result, I think we will try to find a solution that is adequate for today's realities...Who does not evolve, dies."
The International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) has mandatory four-year bans for the most serious doping offences.
Last year, worried by rising legal costs, the IAAF council tried to force a cut in its mandatory bans to two years at its congress but failed after an emotional debate.
However some countries such as Germany have ruled that four-year bans on athletes are illegal under restraint of trade legislation, making such penalties unenforceable.
Former East German sprinter Katrin Krabbe recently won a court battle to overturn a ban, opening the door to German athletes to sue the IAAF if banned long-term.
Other successful legal cases against IAAF-imposed bans by athletes include those of American 400 metres runner Butch Reynolds and British middle-distance runner Diane Modahl.
Two athletes were also allowed to compete in the 1996 Atlanta Olympics despite positive dope tests prior to the Games because sports chiefs were afraid of legal action.
"Sanctions that were around 40 or 50 years ago are no longer any use," insisted de Merode.

"If we have sanctions that are systematically thrown out by the law courts, it is clear that the IOC have learnt nothing and that the fight against doping is lost," he said. "A sanction is only useful in so far as it can be applied."
De Merode said long bans that prevented an athlete from earning a living were no longer acceptable.
He suggested three proposals, starting with short, flexible bans ranging from between one to six months.
These could be accompanied by measures banning the athlete from a certain number of competitions.
"This would have the advantage of losing him or her money, reducing his or her market value but allowing the athlete a way back into the sport," he said.
A second measure would be to impose financial sanctions -- "they don't kill but they hurt," he said.
The third measure would be "educational" in nature, forcing an athlete to remain under special surveillance for a period of up to one year to prove his or her clean status.
"This would be a more modern solution. A fixed sanction is out of date, it is no longer possible today," De Merode said.
He dismissed suggestions of a sea-change in policy at the IOC, saying the proposals were realistic.
Questioned by Reuters on any time frame for new sanctions to be introduced, De Merode was vague. "You know that when you raise new ideas, they have to be discussed," he said.
